Right now, we only have one example of life. The first time we discover life elsewhere in the universe, the main thing we will gain is the ability to compare how life can evolve in different ways. The potential for radically expanding the diversity of the human experience and perspective. Consider the wild diversity of human cultures and lifestyles across the civilizations past to present. The vast assortment of ways we have (or have had) of looking at and experiencing the world, interpreting that experience into language, knowledge, art, music, science, technology. The way these different cultures have evolved, merged, diverged, catalyzed. Now imagine that we suddenly had a whole other venue of this open before us in the exchange with another civilization. To see it all through other, very different, eyes, senses, and a whole other spectrum of cultures and lifestyles. For any truly advanced society the most valuable commodities are novelty and experience and in the meeting of two so totally different societies the resulting creative alchemy could be astounding, regardless of the initial barriers to communication. It would be like finding ten thousand Rosetta Stones, the universe of thought suddenly expanding by an order of magnitude. It would be like the experience of those male children of the isolated Kogi tribe in Colombia who, raised for their first nine years in caves and trained by priests, are first released to the outside world and left with a perpetual state of awe.
